comments.author: @FortuneOfNations
comments.text:
We fixed the bank runs and dumped the gold standard, but we took on $36T in debt to do it. Did we actually solve the problem, or just delay a much bigger crash? What’s your take? 👇

📚 Sources & Data: Every number in this video and where it comes from (in order of appearance):

1. October 1929: the crash. The Dow peaked at 381.17 (Sept 3, 1929) and bottomed at 41.22 (July 8, 1932), down 89%; it got back to its 1929 peak in November 1954 (25 years): https://www.federalreservehistory.org/essays/stock-market-crash-of-1929
2. More than 9,000 U.S. banks failed between 1930 and 1933: https://www.pewresearch.org/short-reads/2023/04/11/most-u-s-bank-failures-have-come-in-a-few-big-waves
3. The economy shrank by nearly a third (real GDP −29% from 1929 to 1933): https://www.stlouisfed.org/the-great-depression/curriculum/economic-episodes-in-american-history-part-3
4. About one worker in four had no job (24.9% estimated unemployment, 1933): https://www.bls.gov/opub/ted/2020/unemployment-rate-rises-to-record-high-14-point-7-percent-in-april-2020.htm
5. April 2020: unemployment jumped to 14.7%, the highest since the series began in 1948: same BLS source as above.
6. December 1930: the Bank of United States in New York fails, about $200 million in deposits, the largest bank failure in U.S. history up to then; many customers were working-class immigrants, and its name led many to think it was backed by the government: https://www.fdic.gov/about/history/deposit-insurance/1930-1939.html · https://ebsco.com/research-starters/history/bank-united-states-fails
7. Depositors lost more than $1.3 billion (1930–1933): FDIC data via Pew, link in 2.
8. March 1933: the national bank holiday closed every bank for a week (March 6–13); FDR's first fireside chat (March 12): "safer to keep your money in a reopened bank than under the mattress": https://www.federalreservehistory.org/essays/bank-holiday-of-1933
9. When banks reopened, people lined up to deposit their money again (the "reverse bank run"): https://libertystreeteconomics.newyorkfed.org/2012/11/historical-echoes-reverse-bank-run-or-when-the-money-came-rollin-in/
10. 1929–1933: the money stock fell by more than a third (Milton Friedman and Anna Schwartz, A Monetary History of the United States, 1963): https://www.nber.org/chapters/c9273.pdf
11. Ben Bernanke, November 8, 2002, speaking to Friedman and Schwartz: "You're right, we did it. We're very sorry. But thanks to you, we won't do it again.": https://www.federalreserve.gov/boarddocs/speeches/2002/20021108/
12. September 1931: Britain leaves the gold standard; in October 1931 the Federal Reserve raised interest rates to stop the gold outflow: https://www.federalreservehistory.org/essays/banking-panics-1931-33
13. January 1930: Japan returns to gold at its old (pre-war) parity; prices fall: https://www.boj.or.jp/en/about/press/koen_2013/ko131028a.htm
14. The Shōwa depression and the devastation of the Japanese countryside: https://www.carf.e.u-tokyo.ac.jp/en/wp-content/uploads/2022/01/comment20090511_asahiglob_en_okazaki.pdf
15. Takahashi Korekiyo (born Sept 19, 1854; 77 in December 1931) takes Japan off gold on his first day as finance minister (December 1931); deficit spending, and from November 1932 the Bank of Japan underwrites new government bonds directly: https://www.ndl.go.jp/portrait/e/datas/122 · https://ideas.repec.org/a/ime/imemes/v21y2003i4p87-103.html
16. Japan among the first major economies to recover (the Bank of Japan says "the first"): BoJ link in 13.
17. The U.S. left gold in April 1933, about a year and a half after Britain; countries that left gold earlier recovered earlier (Eichengreen & Sachs): https://cepr.org/voxeu/columns/end-gold-standard-and-beginning-recovery-great-depression · https://www.nber.org/papers/w1498
18. February 1936: Takahashi is killed by young army officers after trying to curb military spending; he was 81: NDL link in 15.
19. 1933: federal deposit insurance created (FDIC); in 1934 only nine banks failed: https://www.fdic.gov/resources/publications/brief-history-of-deposit-insurance/book/brief-history-deposit-insurance.pdf
20. Deposits insured up to $250,000 per depositor, per bank: https://www.npr.org/2023/03/13/1163138002/the-fdic-insurance-limit-was-last-raised-in-2008-heres-how-it-works
21. March 2023: Silicon Valley Bank customers tried to withdraw $42 billion in one day, the biggest bank run in history; the bank failed the next morning and two days later (March 12) all deposits were guaranteed: https://democrats-financialservices.house.gov/UploadedFiles/HHRG-118-BA00-20230329-SD002.pdf · https://www.axios.com/2023/03/18/silicon-valley-bank-timeline
22. 1971: the dollar's last link to gold is cut (August 15, 1971): https://www.federalreservehistory.org/essays/gold-convertibility-ends
23. September 15, 2008: Lehman Brothers files for bankruptcy; October 2008: TARP, up to $700 billion: https://www.everycrsreport.com/reports/R41427.html
24. The Great Recession: GDP fell 4.3% and unemployment peaked at 10%: https://www.federalreservehistory.org/essays/great-recession-of-200709
25. March 2020: the CARES Act, $2.2 trillion, the largest relief package in U.S. history at the time: https://bc.edu/content/ccc/regulatory-radar/corporate-citizenship-CARES-act-signed-into-law.html
26. Unemployment started falling the very next month (May 2020: 13.3%): https://www.bls.gov/news.release/archives/empsit_06052020.htm
27. 1929: federal debt was less than a fifth of the economy (about 15–16% of GDP, depending on the series): https://www.downsizinggovernment.org/federal-interest-costs-1790-2033
28. Debt held by the public: about 101% of GDP by the end of fiscal 2026, the highest since just after World War II; the record is 106% (1946); projected around 120% by 2036; a deficit of about $1.9 trillion this year; about $1 trillion in interest this year, more than defense, and almost twice defense by 2036: CBO, February 2026 baseline https://budget.house.gov/imo/media/doc/cbo_baseline_february_2026.pdf · GAO https://www.gao.gov/products/gao-26-108610

comments.author: @moneydoodleschannel
comments.text: The contrast that stuck with me was the Fed raising rates in 1931 to defend gold while the economy was collapsing, versus Takahashi taking Japan off gold and spending instead. Same crisis, opposite instincts, and Japan got out first. It made the gold standard feel less like an abstract rule and more like the actual trap.

replies.author: @FortuneOfNations
replies.text: That contrast is the heart of the chapter. Takahashi was 77 when he took the job, and from late 1932 the Bank of Japan was even buying the government's new bonds directly. The sad coda: he was killed in 1936 for trying to rein in military spending.
